mannerism

MAN-uh-riz-um · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Mannerism is a habitual and distinctive gesture or way of behaving or speaking.

Impressionists study a celebrity's every mannerism, from their laugh to the way they hold a coffee cup.

Example

The judge's mannerism of removing her glasses before delivering a verdict became a running joke among the lawyers.

A mannerism is a small, distinctive, repeated habit in how someone behaves or speaks.

Your Turn

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

quirk: A quirk is an odd or unexpected trait — a strange taste, belief, or preference that makes a person distinctive. A mannerism is narrower: a small repeated gesture or way of speaking, something you can watch or hear. Collecting bottle caps is a quirk; drumming your fingers while you think is a mannerism.

affectation: An affectation is a way of acting that someone puts on deliberately to impress others, like a fake accent. A mannerism is genuine and usually unconscious — the person barely notices doing it. If the behavior is a performance for an audience, call it an affectation, not a mannerism.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

plainness: a lack of any distinctive or notable trait

blandness: a lack of any strong or distinctive characteristic

Where it sits · how specific the repeated behavior is

habit → mannerism → tic

habit vs. mannerism: A habit is any routine behavior; a mannerism specifically refers to a small, distinctive gesture or way of speaking.

tic vs. mannerism: A tic often implies an involuntary, almost compulsive small movement, an even more specific and repetitive version of a mannerism.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — manner: a way of doing things (Old French (maniere), from Latin manus, 'hand')

suffix — -ism: a distinctive practice or trait (Greek)

Put it together: manner ('a way of doing things') + -ism ('a distinctive practice') together describe a distinctive, habitual way of behaving.

Use the root in a new word: manual: Manual traces back to the same Latin root manus ('hand') buried deep in manner's own history, though manner itself now stands as its own common English word.
